questions.stem: What does the idiom 'once in a blue moon' mean?

options.option_text: Every night (opposite — blue moon is rare)
Very rarely (correct: 'once in a blue moon' = something that happens very infrequently ✓)
On a cloudy night (literal interpretation — wrong)
Every month (wrong — a 'blue moon' is a second full moon in a month, but the idiom means rarity)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Once in a blue moon' means very rarely or once in a very long while. Origin: a 'blue moon' (second full moon in a month) occurs rarely (~every 2-3 years). Usage: 'He visits his grandparents only once in a blue moon.'

questions.stem: What does 'to beat around the bush' mean?

options.option_text: To hit something physically (literal interpretation — wrong)
To avoid coming to the main point (correct: to speak in a roundabout way, avoiding the core issue ✓)
To work very hard (wrong — 'beat around' means avoid, not work hard)
To search for something in a forest (literal — wrong)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'To beat around the bush' = to avoid saying what you really mean; to talk about unimportant things to avoid the main topic. Origin: hunters would beat bushes to flush out birds rather than going straight for the prey. Usage: 'Stop beating around the bush and tell me directly.'

questions.stem: What does the idiom 'to turn over a new leaf' mean?

options.option_text: To go for a walk in nature (literal leaf — wrong)
To start behaving in a better way; to reform oneself (correct: turning a new page/leaf = fresh start ✓)
To change one's job (work change — not what the idiom means)
To prepare a document (wrong)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Turn over a new leaf' = to make a fresh start and behave in a better or more responsible way. 'Leaf' here refers to a page of a book — turning to a new, blank page. Usage: 'After leaving prison, he decided to turn over a new leaf.'

options.option_text: To eat too fast (eating-related interpretation — wrong)
To be shot (literal — wrong)
To endure a painful or difficult situation with courage (correct: to accept a hard reality and bear it bravely ✓)
To refuse to cooperate (wrong — biting the bullet means accepting, not refusing)

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Bite the bullet' = to endure a painful or difficult situation stoically; to accept the inevitable. Origin: soldiers would bite a bullet to endure the pain of surgery without anaesthesia. Usage: 'We'll have to bite the bullet and cut the budget.'

questions.stem: What does 'to spill the beans' mean?

options.option_text: To cook food carelessly (culinary mistake — wrong)
To accidentally reveal secret information (correct: to let out a secret, either accidentally or deliberately ✓)
To waste resources (wrong)
To be very untidy (wrong)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Spill the beans' = to reveal secret or private information accidentally or prematurely. Usage: 'She spilled the beans about the surprise party before it happened.' Also: 'come clean', 'let the cat out of the bag' are synonymous idioms.

questions.stem: What does the phrase 'on the fence' mean?

options.option_text: Doing physical exercise (fence-jumping — wrong)
Being undecided or neutral on an issue (correct: not having taken a side; being between two positions ✓)
Being in prison (wrong — that's 'behind bars')
Being very careful (wrong)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'On the fence' = not yet decided on an issue; uncommitted; neutral. Image: sitting on a fence between two sides. Usage: 'Many voters are still on the fence about which party to support.' Antonym-ish: 'take a stand', 'take sides'.

questions.stem: What does 'to have a chip on one's shoulder' mean?

options.option_text: To be carrying something heavy (literal — wrong)
To be very happy (wrong — opposite emotion)
To be excessively proud (wrong — chip on shoulder relates to resentment)
To feel resentful or aggrieved about something (correct: to carry a grievance or sense of inferiority ✓)

questions.explanation: D is correct. 'Have a chip on one's shoulder' = to be resentful or touchy, feeling one has been treated unfairly; carrying a grudge. Origin: historically, placing a chip of wood on one's shoulder was a challenge to fight. Usage: 'He has a chip on his shoulder about never getting promoted.'

questions.stem: What does 'at the drop of a hat' mean?

options.option_text: When something falls (literal — wrong)
Without any hesitation; immediately (correct: instantly, at a moment's notice ✓)
After a long wait (opposite meaning)
Very clumsily (wrong)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'At the drop of a hat' = immediately, without any hesitation or prompting. Origin: races or fights that started when a hat was dropped as a signal — so 'at the drop of a hat' means the instant the signal is given. Usage: 'She would help anyone at the drop of a hat.'

questions.stem: What does the idiom 'a blessing in disguise' mean?

options.option_text: A hidden curse (wrong — disguise hides a blessing, not a curse)
Something that seems bad at first but turns out to be good (correct: an apparent misfortune that reveals a hidden benefit ✓)
A very expensive gift (gift-related — wrong)
A religious ceremony (wrong)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'A blessing in disguise' = something that initially seems unfortunate but turns out to be beneficial. Usage: 'Losing that job was a blessing in disguise — it forced him to start his own business.' The key structure: negative appearance, positive reality.

questions.stem: What does 'to burn the midnight oil' mean?

options.option_text: To waste fuel (literal — wrong)
To work or study late into the night (correct: to work until very late at night ✓)
To destroy evidence (wrong)
To celebrate wildly (wrong)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Burn the midnight oil' = to stay up late at night working or studying. Origin: before electricity, lamps burned oil — working past midnight meant literally burning oil into the night. Usage: 'She burned the midnight oil to finish the report before the deadline.'

questions.stem: What does 'to read between the lines' mean?

options.option_text: To read very slowly (literal spacing interpretation — wrong)
To understand the hidden meaning of something written or said (correct: to find the implied, unstated message ✓)
To proofread a document (wrong — proofreading is literal reading)
To read aloud (wrong)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Read between the lines' = to understand what is meant but not explicitly stated; to find hidden or implied meanings. Usage: 'Reading between the lines, it seemed like she was unhappy with the decision even though she didn't say so.'

questions.stem: What does the idiom 'the ball is in your court' mean?

options.option_text: A sports competition is happening (literal sports — wrong)
It is now your turn to take action or make a decision (correct: responsibility for the next move has shifted to you ✓)
You are in a difficult position (wrong — doesn't imply difficulty specifically)
You have already made a mistake (wrong)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'The ball is in your court' = it is now your responsibility to take the next action or make the next decision. From tennis: when the ball lands in your side of the court, it is your turn to hit it. Usage: 'I've made my offer — the ball is in your court now.'
